Fitting a frontier model requires multiple racks versus one GB200 NVL72-class system with 13+ TB of HBM3e. Power is in a similar 100–140 kW range for both. Same power envelope, higher system count and CapEx for Cerebras to achieve model residency that one NVIDIA rack provides natively. Interviews and demos do not alter tokens-per-dollar or tokens-per-watt under realistic multi-tenant loads. The 132 GB ceiling and external I/O bottleneck remain the binding constraints. PR does not rewrite the silicon. $SPY $QQQ $IWM

items.content_excerpt: $AAPL CEO: Yeah, let me give you an overall view on memory. What we’re seeing with memory pricing right now is unprecedented. And as we said earlier, in the September quarter, we did see higher memory costs as compared to the June quarter, which were partly offset by the benefit of carry-in inventory and lower costs on certain non-memory components. Now, for the December quarter, we expect even higher memory costs, partly offset by a few factors. So, as you know, we changed the price on many of our products, including Mac and iPad at the end of June and iPhone in September, and these price increases provided some offset. We also expect to see some benefit from carry-in inventory in the December quarter as well as lower costs on certain non-memory components. And looking beyond the December quarter, we see the pricing for memory purchases continuing to increase. As we’ve said before, we do believe we’ll see a decreasing benefit from the carry-in inventory on memory over time. And there’s one more thing I wanted to add. As we work to improve supply, our manufacturing purchase obligations have increased by $33 billion from June to the September quarter, which you’ll see in our annual filing when it comes out tomorrow. Now, back to Kevan for the other parts of it. $MU $SNDK $DRAM $RAM

items.content_excerpt: $PLTR $SPY $DIA $QQQ $MAGS Palantir earnings are outlining an AI slowdown is right around the corner. Revenue grew 96% from a year earlier, and 20% from the previous quarter, to $2.31 billion, beating analysts’ expectations of $2.18 billion. P reported adjusted earnings per share of 44 cents, compared with analysts’ expectations of 41 cents. The company even raised its revenue guidance, or forecast, for the full year. Palantir’s U.S. commercial revenue surpassed U.S. government revenue for the first time ever. The company reported $984 million in commercial contracts (up 148% from the year-ago quarter), versus $953 million in U.S. government revenue. However, Even as enterprises are moving faster they are signing short-term trials. While the company closed a hefty $1.46 billion of total contract value from U.S. enterprises in the quarter, that’s actually a decline from the record $2.13 billion in the previous quarter. That suggests slowing sales. https://www.bloomberg.com/news/articles/2026-11-02/palantir-boosts-2026-revenue-outlook-on-strong-commercial-sales

items.content_excerpt: $CAPR I reviewed the letter & I'm bullish: - FDA’s own statistician called the key issue a robustness question, not a prespecification one. Leadership can cite that to approve. - FDA admitted it never objected to the imputation rule. Scott said FDA had plenty of time to review SAP 1.7 and didn’t disagree. - FDA narrowed “post hoc” to choices made after SAP 3.0. That’s much narrower than the briefing document’s framing. - The robustness numbers hold up. 28 of 30 primary-endpoint specifications and 104 of 105 single-patient removals stayed below p=0.05, and a model-free test gave about p=0.03. - The powering claim favors Capricor. The trial was powered for 1.1 points, not the 1.5 FDA cited. - It targets the decision-makers. It went straight to Mikhail, Diamantas, and FDA’s chief of staff, and ties a rejection to FDA’s own new rare disease framework. - It pressures against a new trial. All 28 investigators say another placebo trial would be unethical, making a rejection harder to justify.
